title: The USE Method and Flame Graphs: Finding Where Time Actually Goes
objective: Apply Brendan Gregg's USE method to systematically locate a bottlenecked resource, and read a flame graph's width to find the actual expensive code path, instead of guessing at either.

content_blocks.heading: "Make It Faster" Isn't a Starting Point
content_blocks.body:
Optimizing before knowing where time or resources actually go means a real risk of speeding up something that was never the bottleneck, while the actual slow part goes untouched. Two methodologies from Brendan Gregg's systems-performance work solve two different halves of "where do I even look": the USE method narrows down *which resource* is the bottleneck, and flame graphs show *which specific code path* within that resource's usage is actually expensive.

Neither replaces careful thinking about the system -- both exist to replace guessing with a systematic first pass, so the deeper investigation that follows is already pointed at the right place.

The two also have a correct order to run in, which this session builds toward: narrow the resource first, then look inside it, not the other way around -- running them backwards wastes exactly the time they were meant to save in the first place.

content_blocks.heading: The USE Method: Utilization, Saturation, Errors, for Every Resource
content_blocks.body:
The USE method checks three properties for every system resource -- CPU, memory, disk, network -- in a fixed order: Utilization (the percentage of time the resource is busy doing work), Saturation (how much work is queued waiting beyond what the resource can currently handle), and Errors (error events, which can silently degrade performance even without high utilization or saturation). Gregg designed it as a fast checklist, not a deep-dive tool -- something a beginner can run through in minutes, precisely because it's structured and exhaustive rather than relying on which resource happens to look suspicious first.

Running USE systematically catches a real, common failure mode: skipping straight to CPU profiling because that's the familiar tool, while the actual bottleneck is disk I/O saturation that a CPU profile would never reveal, because the CPU was sitting mostly idle waiting on it.

exercises.prompt: A service feels slow under load. An engineer immediately opens a CPU profiler and finds CPU usage sitting at 15%, with no obvious hot function. What does the USE method suggest doing next?

options: Check the other resources too -- disk, memory, network -- since low CPU usage alone doesn't rule any of them out
Conclude the service has no real performance problem at all, since CPU usage alone already came back comfortably low
Profile the CPU even more deeply with a longer sampling window, since 15% usage just needs more sensitive measurement
Assume the 15% CPU figure is simply wrong and switch profilers entirely to get a second, more trustworthy reading
definition.explanation: Low CPU utilization doesn't rule out a bottleneck -- it rules out the CPU specifically. The USE method's whole point is checking every resource systematically rather than stopping at the first, most familiar one: disk I/O saturation, network saturation, or lock contention can all make a service feel slow while CPU usage stays low the entire time, because the CPU is idle waiting, not busy computing.

content_blocks.heading: Utilization and Saturation Are Different Numbers
content_blocks.body:
Utilization measures how busy a resource is on average over a time window -- a disk at 40% utilization sounds like there's plenty of headroom left. Saturation measures queued work beyond what the resource can currently handle -- and a resource can be *low* utilization on average while still being saturated during the specific bursts that actually matter, if the averaging window is wide enough to smooth the spikes out of view.

A disk that's idle most of the second but fully saturated for 200 milliseconds out of every second can report a comfortable 20% average utilization while every request landing in that 200-millisecond window waits in a real queue. Utilization alone, averaged over too wide a window, can hide exactly the saturation that's actually causing the slowness -- which is why USE treats them as two separate properties to check, not one combined number.

Shortening the averaging window, or looking at saturation metrics (queue depth, wait time) directly instead of utilization alone, is usually what actually surfaces this kind of hidden bottleneck.

exercises.prompt: A disk reports 20% utilization averaged over one-second windows, yet requests are intermittently slow. What does this combination most likely indicate?

options: The disk is briefly saturated during short bursts that a one-second average is too coarse to reveal on its own
The reported utilization figure must simply be incorrect, since a genuinely bottlenecked disk cannot show 20% usage
The slowness has nothing to do with the disk at all, since its utilization is clearly far too low to be the cause
Saturation and utilization always move together in lockstep, so low utilization guarantees low saturation as well
definition.explanation: Utilization averaged over a wide window can smooth away short, intense bursts of saturation -- the disk might be fully queued for 200ms out of every second and still average out to a comfortable-looking 20% over the full second. This is exactly why USE checks saturation as its own separate property instead of assuming low average utilization rules out a real bottleneck.

content_blocks.heading: Flame Graphs: Width Is Time, Not Depth
content_blocks.body:
Once USE points at CPU as the actual bottleneck, a flame graph shows which specific code path is spending that CPU time. Each frame is one function on the call stack; a frame's vertical position shows stack depth (how deeply nested the call is), but its *width* is what actually encodes time -- the proportion of profiling samples where that function was on the stack. A wide frame near the bottom means that function (or something it calls) accounts for a large share of the total CPU time sampled, regardless of how deep in the call stack it sits.

The common misreading is scanning for the *tallest* tower, assuming the deepest call chain must be the expensive one -- but depth only shows how many calls are nested, not how much time any of them actually took. A short, wide frame near the base of the graph can represent far more real CPU time than a narrow, deeply-nested spike that looks visually dramatic but barely registers in the sample count.

exercises.prompt: Looking at a flame graph, an engineer focuses on the tallest, most deeply-nested tower of frames, assuming it must be the most expensive code path. What's the actual signal that indicates where CPU time is really going?

options: Frame width -- the proportion of samples a function appears in -- not how deep or tall its call stack happens to be
Frame height exclusively -- the deepest, tallest call stack always corresponds to the function consuming the most time
The color assigned to each frame, which flame graphs use specifically to encode exact CPU time in milliseconds
The left-to-right horizontal position of a frame, which encodes when during the profiling run that call occurred
definition.explanation: Width is the one dimension flame graphs use to encode time -- the share of profiling samples in which a function was on the call stack. A deep, narrow tower might represent a rare, quick code path that happened to nest many calls; a short, wide frame near the base can represent a function consuming far more actual CPU time, simply by being on the stack in a much larger share of samples.

content_blocks.heading: The Two Methods Are Complementary, Not Competing
content_blocks.body:
USE and flame graphs answer different questions in sequence, not two alternative ways to answer the same one. USE narrows the search from "the whole system" down to "this specific resource is actually bottlenecked" -- CPU, disk, memory, or network. A flame graph then only makes sense once CPU specifically has already been identified as the bottleneck; running one against a system that's actually disk-saturated just profiles CPU time that was never the problem in the first place.

The practical order is always USE first, flame graph second: skipping straight to a flame graph without first confirming CPU is the actual bottleneck risks spending real investigation time understanding a detailed, accurate picture of a resource that was never slow.

The same ordering logic generalizes beyond these two specific tools: confirm the right category of problem before investing effort in a detailed tool built for one specific category.

exercises.prompt: A team captures a detailed CPU flame graph before checking whether CPU is actually the bottlenecked resource. The real bottleneck turns out to be network saturation. What did skipping the USE-method step cost them?

options: Real investigation time spent on an accurate, detailed picture of a resource that was never actually the problem
Nothing of consequence -- a flame graph is equally informative regardless of which resource is the real bottleneck
The flame graph itself would have been technically impossible to generate without first running the USE method
This mistake only ever matters for systems running under 1% CPU utilization; above that, ordering makes no difference
definition.explanation: A flame graph answers "where in the CPU-bound code is time going," which is simply the wrong question when the system is actually network-saturated and CPU was never the bottleneck -- it can still render a perfectly detailed, accurate CPU breakdown, just one that doesn't explain the real slowness at all. Running USE first would have pointed straight at the network instead, skipping the wasted detour entirely.

content_blocks.heading: The Bottom Line
content_blocks.body:
The USE method is a fast, systematic checklist -- utilization, saturation, and errors, for every resource -- that narrows down which resource is actually the bottleneck before any deep profiling starts. A flame graph then shows exactly where within that resource's usage the time goes, using frame *width*, not depth, as the signal that actually encodes time spent. Run in that order, together they replace guessing with a structured path from "something is slow" to "this specific function, confirmed by the actual bottlenecked resource."

Both tools reward the same habit: check broadly and systematically before diving deep into any one area, since the area that looks suspicious first isn't reliably the one that's actually the problem.

The next sessions in this module get concrete about what causes CPU time to concentrate the way a flame graph reveals: allocation patterns, garbage collection pauses, and the blocking/contention that shows up as time spent waiting rather than computing.
